plain_language: Indiana local governments have broad home rule: they may use any power the law grants plus any other power they need to run their affairs, unless the state limits it.
detail: The Home Rule Act (1980) ended Dillon's Rule. Doubts about a unit's power are decided in favor of the unit. A unit generally may not regulate conduct that a state agency regulates unless a statute allows it (limits are in IC 36-1-3-8, not read). Cedar Lake v. Alessia (Ind. Ct. App. 2013) held a trial court erred by applying Dillon's Rule. Whether the Act applies to townships the same way was not checked.

plain_language: Property tax bills are capped by the Indiana Constitution at 1% of assessed value for a homestead, 2% for other residential property and farmland, and 3% for other real property and business personal property.
detail: Art. 10 sec. 1(f): 1% for a principal residence; 2% for other residential property and agricultural land; 3% for other real property and personal property. The statute adds long-term care property to the 2% group. If a bill is higher, the taxpayer gets a credit; the county auditor applies it without an application, and the lost revenue falls on the local taxing units, not the state. Taxes approved by voters in a referendum, and certain older debt payments, are not counted toward the cap. Voters approved the constitutional amendment in November 2010; the statutory credit applies to taxes first due after 2009. A 2026 Senate joint resolution proposed changes to Section 1; its status was not checked.

plain_language: A local unit's property tax levy can grow each year only by a limit set by state formula (the maximum levy growth quotient).
detail: The State Budget Agency calculates the quotient each year. The Department of Local Government Finance (DLGF) checks that adopted levies are within the legal maximums and can certify a lower budget if a unit goes over. A unit can ask DLGF for a levy appeal.

plain_language: The Department of Local Government Finance (DLGF) reviews and certifies local budgets, tax rates and levies, and publishes local budget data on the Gateway site.
detail: DLGF also handles additional appropriations, local debt, local income tax, referendums and tax increment financing (TIF) information, and forms for assessment appeals (taxpayers appeal to the county first). The exact statutory text of its budget approval power was not read; it is described here from DLGF presentations and statute excerpts.

plain_language: In most Indiana counties the county council controls spending, taxes and borrowing, and the board of commissioners handles county property, roads, contracts and board appointments.
detail: Some counties differ by statute: the state county-government brochure says a few counties vest full legislative power in the council. That list of counties and the statute were not checked.

plain_language: Most counties elect a county council of 4 district members and 3 at-large members. Counties of 185,000 to 300,000 people could opt in, by resolution before September 1, 2023, to nine single-member council districts and three single-member commissioner districts.
detail: Opt-in counties elect all nine council members by single-member district (three nested in each commissioner district). Whether a given county opted in is shown in its own edition. The research had reversed the council structure and has been corrected.

plain_language: Indiana sorts cities by population: first class is 600,000 or more, second class is 34,000 to 599,999, third class is under 34,000. Any other municipality is a town.
detail: A city that reaches 34,000 stays second class even if its population later falls below that figure, and its council may choose third-class status by ordinance. Second-class city councils have district and at-large seats.

plain_language: A township has one elected trustee and a three-member township board. The trustee runs township services and the board approves the budget.
detail: Services documented on township sites include help for people in need (poor relief), fire protection, cemeteries and parks. The trustee must live in the township and serves a four-year term starting January 1 after the election.

plain_language: Under a 2026 law, some townships will have to consolidate with a city or town, or merge with another township, in 2027 and 2028.
detail: Applies to townships that the DLGF assigns a certain number of points; the former township government is dissolved when the process ends. SEA 270 (P.L. 134-2026).

plain_language: In 2025 the state passed Senate Enrolled Act 1, which cut property taxes for homeowners (ABC57 summarized it as $1.3 billion in relief over three years) and changed local income taxes. Local governments say it reduces their revenue.
detail: Reported provisions include a new homestead credit, changes to deductions, a higher business personal property exemption and a rewrite of local income tax rules. Estimated lost local revenue is $1.4 billion over 2026-2028, per the Capital Chronicle; ABC57 summarized it as $1.3 billion in property tax relief to homeowners over three years. Dollar impact on any one unit is shown in its edition.

plain_language: SEA 1 created a homestead credit of 10% of the tax bill, up to $300, starting in 2026, with an extra $150 for qualifying low-income seniors.
detail: Sources agree on the credit; details were not checked against the enrolled text.

plain_language: SEA 1, as amended by HEA 1427 (2025), raised the business personal property exemption from $80,000 to $1 million for the 2025 assessment date and $2 million from the 2026 assessment date.
SEA 1 phases down the standard homestead deduction while raising the supplemental deduction, but sources disagree on the schedule.
detail: One guide gives $40,000 in 2026, then $30,000, $20,000 and $10,000, ending in 2030, with the supplemental deduction rising to 66.7% by 2031. The Journal Gazette gives different timing. Check the enrolled text before relying on any year.

plain_language: Local income tax (LIT) councils end on July 1, 2027, and the county fiscal body becomes the body that sets LIT; the maximum total LIT rate becomes 2.9%, and cities and towns can adopt a municipal LIT within that total.
detail: The rate changes originally started in 2028; HEA 1210 (2026) delayed them to 2029. The municipal LIT share is up to 1.2% within the county total per the Capital Chronicle; a population threshold for cities and towns was not confirmed. The elimination of LIT property-tax-relief credits was reported for 2028 before the delay; its current date was not checked.

plain_language: HEA 1210 (2026), the DLGF omnibus bill, delayed SEA 1's local income tax changes from 2028 to 2029, allowed a county and its municipalities to form a 'Municipal Unit Strategic Taskforce,' and ordered a study committee.
detail: Signed March 12, 2026; P.L. 157-2026. It also changes how political subdivisions publish required notices, from July 1, 2027. The research's statement that it expands disabled-veteran relief is not supported and is not encoded. Note: the effective date 2026-03-12 is the signing date reported by the Capital Chronicle, not a confirmed effective date. The Secretary of State summary confirms P.L. 157-2026 and a July 1, 2027 effective date for the notice sections but does not state the effective date of the LIT-delay sections.

plain_language: State 'tuition support' is the largest part of the state budget. Each school corporation gets a per-student foundation amount plus added grants for low-income students, special education, career and technical education and other purposes.
detail: Curricular materials (about $158 per student) moved into the formula for 2025-26. Appropriations were about $9.4 billion in FY2026 and $9.7 billion in FY2027 (one source gives $9.6 billion for 2026-27).

plain_language: Under SEA 1, some school operating levy revenue is shared with charter schools. ABC57 reported in December 2025 that School City of Mishawaka could lose more than $1 million by 2028 as a result.
detail: School City of Mishawaka reported it could lose more than $1 million by 2028 (ABC57, Dec 2025).

plain_language: Public library boards are appointed by other local units (such as school boards, the county council and county commissioners), not elected.
detail: Trustees generally serve four-year terms with a limit of four consecutive terms, per the State Library blog; not re-read. Library districts levy property tax in Indiana (not verified in the sources).

plain_language: A county has a circuit court and may have superior courts, a probate court and small claims courts set up by statute; the mix varies by county.
detail: Circuit judges are elected in partisan races to 6-year terms (state brochure). Superior court judges in four counties are chosen by merit selection (see election_rules). Number of superior court judges in any county is shown in its edition.
